paper.title: PENNING AND ASSOCIATIVE IONIZATION IN COLLISIONS OF LASER-EXCITED Na ATOMS WITH K ATOMS
paper.affiliation: Department of Physics, Faculty of Science, Osaka University, Toyonaka, Osaka 564 Japan

goals: Observe Penning ionization (Na* + K → Na + K⁺ + e⁻) and associative ionization (Na* + K → NaK⁺ + e⁻) in collisions of laser-excited Na atoms with K atoms
Measure ionization cross sections for various excited Na levels
Study laser-induced collisional ionization under intense and weak laser fields

intermediate.Na*: excited levels populated by two-step laser excitation: 3s → 3p (laser I, Na D₁ line) then 3p → ns/nd (laser II)

potential_curves.ground_state_NaK⁺: estimated from photoionization data (Foster et al. [7]) and dissociation energy (Huber & Herzberg [8]), modified from theoretical calculation by Valance [9]

models: Potential energy curves for Na-K system (Fig. 2)
Laser-induced collisional ionization (photon absorption by quasi-molecule)

calculations.Valance_1978: Theoretical potential curve of NaK⁺ (J. Chem. Phys. 69 (1978) 355)

theory.interpretation: Results interpreted via potential energy curves of electronically excited (Na-K)* and ground-state (Na-K)⁺ systems, but information is insufficient

quantities.description: Time-of-flight spectra of product ions (K⁺, NaK⁺, Na⁺, Na₂⁺, K₂⁺)
Relative intensities of K⁺, NaK⁺, Na⁺, Na₂⁺, K₂⁺ under various laser/beam conditions

findings: Penning ionization (K⁺ production) observed for Na(6d), Na(7s), Na(5d), Na(6s) but NOT for Na(4d) and Na(5s) due to insufficient energy (threshold 0.46 eV higher than associative)
Associative ionization (NaK⁺ production) observed for all excited levels EXCEPT Na(4d)-K system
NaK⁺ signals are less than 10⁻¹ of K⁺ signals when both observed
Na(4d)-K associative ionization signal especially small, suggesting highly repulsive potential curve or barrier at large internuclear separation
Control experiments (Fig. 4) confirm K⁺ and NaK⁺ arise solely from collisions of highly excited Na(6d) with ground-state K
Na⁺ produced via resonance-enhanced three-photon photoionization (requires both lasers tuned to Na transitions)
Na₂⁺ originates from ionization of Na₂(B ¹Πᵤ) by laser II radiation
K₂⁺ formation mechanism similar to Na₂⁺, via laser II excitation of K₂ to B ¹Πᵤ state
results.conclusions: Under present experimental conditions (weak laser field), K⁺ and NaK⁺ are produced only through collisions of highly excited Na atoms with ground-state K atoms. More detailed studies needed, especially cross-section measurements as function of energy states and laser-induced ionization under intense fields.

fig1.caption: Schematic drawing of the apparatus
fig1.content: Crossed Na and K beams, two collinear dye laser beams, copper baffle with liquid-nitrogen trap, ion extraction at 90° to beam plane, electron multiplier 19 cm from collision center

fig2.caption: Potential energies of the Na-K system. Two stepwise excitations of Na by lasers are shown by arrows.
fig2.content: Potential minimum of ground-state NaK⁺ estimated from photoionization data and dissociation energy; pumping actions of lasers I and II indicated

fig3.caption: TOF spectra of product ions. Time scale 2 μs/div. Laser II tuned to: (a) 3p-6d, (b) 3p-4d, (c) 3p-5s transitions of Na.
fig3.content: Shows K⁺ and NaK⁺ signals for Na(6d)-K, Na(4d)-K, Na(5s)-K collision systems

fig4.caption: TOF spectra of product ions for Na(6d)-K system under various conditions. Time scale 2 μs/div. (a) All beams on, laser II at 3p-6d. (b) Laser II off-tuned <5 Å. (c) Na, K, laser I on; laser II off. (d) Either laser II off, or Na off. (e) K off.
fig4.content: Control experiments identifying formation mechanisms of K⁺, NaK⁺, Na⁺, Na₂⁺, K₂⁺

limitations: Insufficient information about potential energy curves of electronically excited (Na-K)* and ground-state (Na-K)⁺ systems
Cross sections for reactions (1) and (2) not measured as function of relevant energy states of Na
Laser-induced ionization processes under intense laser field not yet studied
Na(4d) associative ionization signal too small to quantify, suggesting need for theoretical potential curves
